item.title: Why is Shabana Mahmood tackling ‘two-tier policing’ if she doesn’t believe it exists? | Gaby Hinsliff
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Ten years ago this month, Stephen Port was convicted of the murders of four young gay men lured to their deaths via the dating app Grindr.

But it took another five years for their families to learn through an inquest what some had long suspected: that the Metropolitan police’s failure to link the murders quickly enough may have contributed to the later deaths, raising difficult questions over whether that would have happened if the victims were straight. The year after that, officers at Charing Cross station were caught WhatsApping each other rape jokes and insults like “fuck you bender”, contributing to Louise Casey’s conclusion in a review not long afterwards that the force was both institutionally homophobic and misogynistic.

There have been extremely good reasons for the decision many forces across Britain made to let uniformed police officers march openly at Pride events in recent years, rather than simply stewarding. It seemed a quick, tangible way of signalling that times have changed, that hate crimes will be taken seriously and that gay officers are welcome to serve or join. But in a case brought against Northumbria police last year by a lesbian arguing that gender critical activists had been made to feel unwelcome at Pride, a judge ruled that Pride had become so politically contested that marching breached impartiality rules, warning other forces to take note. This week, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, made clear that she supported that ban. Some forces had drifted “out of the realm of policing and into the world of politics” in trying to engage the public, she told police commissioners, suggesting in future they stick to “tea and biscuits” with residents’ associations rather than hanging out with activists.

That sideswipe came as Mahmood made a speech announcing plans to tackle so-called two-tier policing – the false and inflammatory idea that the police routinely and deliberately go soft on ethnic minority offenders. These plans have been undeniably complicated by the fact that, as Mahmood herself acknowledged, there’s no evidence that the problem actually exists outside Nigel Farage’s imagination. Her solution was to scrap a police statement on anti-racism principles that Reform UK made hay with in the wake of the tragic murder of Henry Nowak, the teenager unforgivably handcuffed by police as he was dying of stab wounds because they mistook him for the assailant rather than the victim.

The statement argues that equality “does not mean treating everyone the same”, an established principle in anti-discrimination law (forcing a pregnant woman to lift the same heavy boxes as everyone else working in your warehouse is technically equal treatment, but that doesn’t make it fair). Though there’s no evidence that it directly affected the officers’ decisions the night of Nowak’s murder, and Mahmood acknowledged she could see what it was trying to achieve, she insisted that the public find it “patently absurd”, and she wasn’t about to argue with them. So there will be a new impartiality code, including rules on avoiding politicised symbols – another Reform gripe is LGBTQ+-friendly rainbow markings on police cars – and on engaging with the public, which is where Pride marches come in.

Police should, she argued, beware “misguided attempts at course corrections” made while scrabbling to keep up with culture wars. Though if the police seem confused, they’ve arguably only been reflecting successive governments, who have done their share of handbrake turns over LGBTQ+ rights.

What Mahmood was trying to do this week was one of the hardest tasks in politics, which is to side with the public on an issue where the public is hopelessly divided. Plenty of Britons now believe two-tier policing exists, according toYouGov research this summer; unfortunately, they disagree on who is in which tier. Over half think black people are singled out for differential treatment, but they’re more likely to say this treatment is extra strict than extra lenient. A third think the police come down harder on people with far-right views, but one in five think they’re harder on people with far-left views. And though 25% think white people get a uniquely raw deal, exactly the same number think they have it easier, with a marked tendency for people to think their own group is especially hard done by. (Though YouGov didn’t poll LGBTQ+ people specifically, Stonewall research suggests one in four of those who had experienced a hate crime and not reported it said it was because they didn’t trust the police.) It’s hard to draw any firm conclusions except that distrust of the police is remarkably widespread; but evidently that’s not the story either Reform or Labour wants to tell.

If Mahmood looks increasingly out of step with a cabinet that has shifted at least rhetorically to the left under Andy Burnham, that’s in part just the nature of being a Labour home secretary. Since Labour never gets the benefit of the doubt over law and order, its home secretaries end up forced into taking the hardest possible line on law and order so that nobody can say they’re soft on it. But there is another difference between Mahmood and her new boss emerging, and it’s about the willingness to make an argument.

If the public fervently believe something that you think is nonsense, is your job to agree with them or to bust the myth? On Brexit, Burnham chose the latter, pointing out politely but firmly that it hasn’t worked out. But Mahmood seems to be choosing the former, cracking down on a “perception” of injustice she freely admits is a chimera. The trouble with boxing shadows is that sooner or later, the wrong person risks getting punched in the face.

- Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-21 06:00 UTC

item.title: 5 Famous Books That Were Written Under the Influence of Drugs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

You might think that taking drugs wouldnât be conducive to writing a good book, but there are actually a few famous novels that defy that idea. There are some books that clearly owe a debt to the authorâs drug habitâThe Doors of Perception (1954) by Aldous Huxley and Naked Lunch (1959) by William S. Burroughs being two of the most famous examplesâbut there are a few other titles that unexpectedly fall into this category. Here are five such books that were surprisingly written (at least partly) by authors who were under the influence of drugsâranging from peyote to cocaine.

Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886) // Robert Louis Stevenson

Robert Louis Stevenson suffered from chronic lung problems for most of his life and itâs thought that the drugs he took to ease his symptomsâhe had trouble breathing and would cough up bloodâmay have actually aided his creative process. In 1885, the Treasure Island (1883) author was taking cocaine and a hallucinogenic called ergotine. He was in a drug-induced stupor one night when his wife, Fanny, woke him up from a nightmare. âWhy did you wake me?â he complained. âI was dreaming a fine bogey tale.â

That âbogey taleâ inspired Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hydeâthe first draft of which Stevenson frantically wrote over the course of just three days. That version ended up being thrown into the fire because the allegory wasnât strong enough, but whether it was Stevenson or Fanny who destroyed the pages remains uncertain. He then spent another three days frenziedly rewriting the now iconic horror novella.

On the Road (1957) // Jack Kerouac

Literary legend has it that Beat Generation writer Jack Kerouac wrote the first draft of his seminal novel On the Road on a 120-foot-long scroll in one feverish burst that lasted three weeksâa feat that was sustained by amphetamines (specifically Benzedrine). But while Kerouacâs use of the stimulant is accurate, the real story of the novelâs creation is a little more complicated.

Kerouac first noted down his idea for the novel in August 1948: âtwo guys hitchhiking to California in search of something they donât really find, and losing themselves on the road, coming all the way back hopeful of something else.â He wrote up a few drafts, but struggled to find the right prose style for the story. Then at the end of 1950, he received a rambling freeform letter from his friend Neal Cassady (who inspired the character Dean Moriarty) and realized it was the exact style he was looking for. Kerouac dubbed it âspontaneous proseâ and, armed with thorough notes and Benzedrine, he then sat down to bash out On the Road on the huge scroll.

Cujo (1981) // Stephen King

Stephen King isnât shy about his former substance abuse problem, telling Rolling Stone in a 2014 interview that he was a heavy cocaine user from around 1978 to 1986 and would often write while high and drunk. This means that a number of his most famous books were written under the influenceâincluding Cujo (1981), Pet Sematary (1983), and IT (1986). âI barely remember writing [Cujo] at all,â he admits in his memoir, On Writing (2000). âI donât say that with pride or shame, only with a vague sense of sorrow and loss.â But although King managed to produce some masterpieces during this drug-fuelled time, he told Rolling Stone that âthe books start to show it after a while.â He cites The Tommyknockersâwhich was the last book he wrote before quitting cokeâas one of his worst books.

One Flew Over the Cuckooâs Nest (1962) // Ken Kesey

In 1959, Ken Keseyâthen a student at Stanford Universityâvolunteered to take part in MK-Ultra, a drug research program being run by the CIA. Participants were given psychoactive drugs, including LSD, psilocybin, and mescaline. While high in the ward, Kesey looked around and began to wonder: âWhatâs the difference between the orderlies and the nurse and the patients?â His wife, Faye Kesey McMurtry, recalls that âhe began to see that they were all damaged in some way or another.â Not only did the experience help to inspire One Flew Over the Cuckooâs Nest (as did actually working on a psychiatric ward), but he also liked LSD so much that he continued taking it. The first three pages of the novelâwhich was adapted into an Oscar-winning 1975 film starring Jack Nicholsonâwere also written while Kesey was high on peyote.

Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968) // Philip K. Dick

Philip K. Dickâs literary career kicked off in the early 1950s, and from the very beginning his writing was fuelled by amphetamines. In a 1975 interview with Rolling Stone, the sci-fi author said that every novel heâd written up until A Scanner Darkly (1977) was done so with the aid of speed. This means that his most famous book, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?âwhich in 1982 was adapted into a film by Ridley Scott under the title Blade Runnerâwas written while he was on drugs.

âI believed there was a direct connection between the amphetamines and the writing,â Dick explained in the Rolling Stone interview. âI attributed my speed of writing, my high productivity and my pushing myself to the amphetamines.â Throughout the â60s, he also took mescaline, marijuana, LSD, and PCP. His doctor warned him that his liver was at risk of collapse and he eventually kicked the habit (although he had already done permanent damage to his pancreas). Fortunately his creative output didnât suffer in the long run though, and he continued publishing until his death in 1982.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-21 02:00 UTC

item.title: 5 Things You Probably Didn't Know About Artemis, the Greek Goddess of the Hunt
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

More gods from the Greek pantheon are making an appearance in Percy Jackson and the Olympians season 3. Chief among them is Artemis. In the series, her presence is tied to an invitation that she extends to Annabeth Chaseâone that would shift the young demigodâs allegiance to the goddess of the hunt and put her on a path that Percy and Grover cannot walk with her.

In Greek mythology, Artemis holds dominion over the wilderness and wild animals. She is associated with the moon and considered to be both a harmonious and opposing force to her twin brother, Apollo, the god of prophecy and music who is associated with the sun.

Most know Artemis by her hunting bow and quiver of arrows, though sheâs sometimes draped in a deerskin cape complete with a hood or crowned with a diadem. Famously, she is a virgin goddess whose followers pledge chastity and are held to living pure lives under penalty of severe punishment.

But what might you not know about her? Letâs get into some of the long-held and most disputed beliefs behind the goddessâ origins, meaning, and actions, according to ancient Greek stories that have stood the test of time.

Artemis Delivered Her Twin Brother Apollo

The Titaness Leto is the mother of Artemis and Apollo. Her affair with Zeus, which produced a pregnancy, angered the goddess Heraâthe Queen of the Gods and Zeusâ wifeâso violently that she forbade Leto from giving birth on land or in water. To ensure Leto adhered to her order, the giant serpent Python was commanded to pursue Leto throughout her pregnancy. She was given no leave to rest as nowhere was safe.

Fortunately for Leto, she came upon Delos. The floating island allowed her to stay within the bounds of Heraâs words. First, she gave birth to Artemis. Then, according to some versions of the myth, her daughter served as her midwife and delivered her twin into the world. That is why Artemis is a goddess of childbirth along with her many other duties.

The Goddess of the Hunt Loves to Dance

Artemis is primarily thought of as a huntress. Her youth, athleticism, and vigor are typically visible in depictions of her, and she is also often portrayed alongside animals, her trusty silver-and-gold bow and quiver of arrows in hand. But, like Apollo, she also loves music, and that includes dancing to it with the nymphs in her retinue.

Her worshippers often honor her through choral dance, a style of rhythmic movement that is coordinated and done in unison. It includes singing and vocalization, and participants often run and mimic animals in devotion to the goddess.

Artemis Is Both the Protector and Bringer of Death to Girls

In antiquity, Artemis was portrayed as a maiden because she is considered to be the protector of girls up until they marry. While her charge is their safety, that does not mean she always keeps girls from harm.Â

As is true of the rest of the Grecian gods, Artemis can be fickle. She can act in favor of one mortal, healing their wounds and ending their suffering, while bringing ruin through sudden death or disease to another.

She Is Responsible for the Constellation Orion

Though the prevailing belief is that Artemis has never fallen in love, she had a close companion in Orion. The giant huntsman skilled with weaponry had earned her respect so deeply that Apollo grew jealous, and tricked his sister into shooting her friend. Grief-stricken, she laid Orion to rest among the stars.

Some stories suggest Apollo betrayed Artemis to protect her vow of chastity as she was in love with Orion. Others claim that she purposefully shot the giant because heâd attempted to assault her or one of her attendants, and in these stories, there is no mention of her making him a constellation.

Artemis Is Incredibly Vengeful

Blessed with the power to transform herself and anyone she chooses into an animal, Artemis has also been said to use her abilities to punish those who incur her wrath.Â

When her handmaiden Callisto was seduced by Zeus after he took the goddessâs form, Artemis turned her into a bear after learning of Callistoâs pregnancy. She then banished her to the wild.

The hunter Actaeon suffered a worse fate. Artemis transformed him into a stag after she caught him watching her bathe in a spring with her nymphs. She set his hounds on him, and they tore Actaeon apart.

There was also Niobe, queen of Thebes, whose children and husband bore the consequences of her boastfulness. She had compared her 14 children to Letoâs twins, and the slight drew Artemis and Apolloâs ire. They killed all seven of her sons and her seven daughters as well. The pain of the loss resulted in Niobeâs husband also dying, though itâs disputed whether he killed himself or was slain to ensure he didnât try to avenge their children.

Niobe was turned to stone, either in pity by the gods or because her devastation was so great that it literally petrified her. However, the transformation didnât stop her tears, which continued to fall from her eyes.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-21 00:00 UTC

item.title: If Democrats want to win, blue-collar populists are the key | Dustin Guastella and Jared Abbott
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Democrats had a huge night on 3 November. The party ran an average of about 15 points ahead of Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins, and picked up seats that Trump carried by double digits just two years ago.

Of course, the size and scope of the blue wave make it hard to draw specific lessons, and the results will inevitably serve as a Rorschach test reflecting each commentator’s prior beliefs. Democrats of all stripes won elections in all sorts of unlikely places.

But it would be a big mistake to assume that because all sorts of Democrats won big in 2026 thanks to a backlash against Trump, any Democrat will do in 2028. There is now a decade of experience, 2026 notwithstanding, showing us that “I’m not Trump” is not the slam dunk Democrats want it to be.

That’s to say Democrats still need a program and political pitch for 2028. One way to get a sense of what might be the best way forward is to look at which candidates did best relative to their districts’ political lean, demographic makeup and other Democrats.

And here is the big story of the night: neither the down-the-line professional-class progressives nor the corporate-sponsored centrists did as well as the working-class populists who have a bold economic vision for working people but also know how to talk to workers.

Before we dig into those results, first, some cold water.

Despite Democrats’ big night, the party is still doing badly with working-class voters.

That matters because not only is this group the largest in the electorate (57% of 2026 voters lacked a four-year degree), it is also a swing group. In 2024, voters without a college degree swung seven points toward Trump, from a six-point Republican margin in 2020 to a 13-point one. In 2026, they swung back hard, by 17 points.

Still, Democrats won college graduates by 26 points and voters without degrees by just four points, leaving a 22-point education gap, and they lost white voters without degrees by 19 points.

If Democrats want to win a commanding and durable majority, one capable of implementing their progressive economic plans and finally delivering for working Americans, they will need to do better with these voters.

The question is, what kind of Democrat can do it?

Progressives have long argued that they are the Democrats best suited to winning back the working class, but the results in 2026 don’t bear this out – at least not in a straightforward way.

In general, though they of course performed well overall, the most liberal candidates fared worse compared with their centrist counterparts. Nominees backed by Justice Democrats ran about one point behind our estimate of how a typical Democrat would have done in the same district, given its 2024 presidential vote, demographics and whether an incumbent was running (a statistic known as “wins above replacement”, or War), and Bernie Sanders’s Senate endorsees ran about six and a half points behind.

As a result, centrists have taken to social media to crow about how their brand of politics is more suited to building majorities. But here they might be overstepping, especially when it comes to the question of social class.

Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast tweeted: “The whole theory that to expand the map that Dems had to nominate working classoids who dress in Carhartts just seems totally obliterated.” Is that true? Hardly.

As it happens, blue-collar populists such as Brian Poindexter (a union ironworker in Ohio), Bob Brooks (a firefighter in Pennsylvania), Sam Forstag (a former smokejumper in Montana) and Rebecca Cooke (a waitress in Wisconsin), who were all backed by both Bernie Sanders and the moderate Blue Dog Democrats, as well as Randy Villegas (a community college professor from California’s Central valley), outperformed both professional-class progressives backed by Sanders and progressive Pacs – such as Abdul El-Sayed (a doctor) and Peggy Flanagan (a non-profit executive turned lieutenant governor) – and centrists backed by the New Democrat Coalition, such as Tom Suozzi and Jared Moskowitz.

Compared with our estimate of a typical Democrat’s performance, Poindexter ran almost 11 points ahead, Forstag about five, Cooke about four and Brooks about two, for an average of about +5, compared with about +2 for nominees backed only by the Blue Dogs and about even for those backed only by Sanders. Villegas, whose race is still being counted, ran about 14 points ahead.

El-Sayed and Flanagan ran five and six points behind, and Suozzi and Moskowitz trailed by one and a half and six points, respectively. As a group, the four Blue Collar Brigade nominees (Poindexter, Villegas, Forstag and Brooks), union-backed working-class candidates who ran as a slate, averaged a War of nearly +8, and all four ran ahead of comparable Democrats, by about eight points on average.

No other progressive or centrist group’s nominees averaged better than about +3.

In fact, the sweet spot looks like the vaunted “Bernie-dog” candidate who leans left on wages, jobs and the economy, is good at talking about those issues in plain language, and steers toward the center on issues like immigration and criminal justice.

These are candidates who are justifiably frustrated with trade deals that shipped their communities’ jobs overseas, who value patriotism and tradition while sticking up for the working class against the economic giants that are grinding them into dust.

Plus, it really does matter when populist candidates come from the popular classes. While professional-class progressives, like El-Sayed, soak up a lot of media attention, and moderates like Jon Ossoff clean up with donors, blue-collar candidates remain underappreciated for their ability to break through.

Social class remains a major issue unto itself and blue-collar populists are uniquely able to tap into the frustrations of blue-collar voters.

Just look at Troy Jackson, the soon-to-be senator from Maine. Jackson was subject to a late-campaign attack ad that questioned his competence by virtue of his background. Susan Collins’s now-infamous “cord of wood” ad implied that Jackson was better suited to logging than legislating.

That kind of visceral class condescension makes the Gilded Age economy much more real for voters and could have shifted his margins in a favorable direction. Jackson succeeded in unseating the supposedly untouchable Susan Collins.

It’s not clear what direction the Democratic party will go in the future but one thing is certain: blue-collar populists are still the most underrated current in the party and if the bigwigs want to win back working-class voters, they really ought to start investing in candidates who are used to showering at the end of the day rather than in the morning.

- Dustin Guastella is a research associate at the Center for Working Class Politics and the director of operations for Teamsters Local 623

- Jared Abbott is the director of the Center for Working-Class Politics

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-20 15:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/20/democrats-blue-collar-populists

item.title: Is it genuine love – or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation – these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don’t want to let that person out of your sight.

It’s the start of many happy love stories. But at times, that feeling of obsession never fades – and the relationship never matures, or it even proves harmful. You know the relationship is bad for you, but you can’t end it. The more you try to break free, the more you feel stuck.

As a counselor, I often work with people whose relationships feel like an addiction, and who mistake that emotional roller coaster for love. And as a philosopher, I sometimes turn to 19th-century Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard to reflect on the differences between the two.

Kierkegaard is best known for his writing on religion. Today, he’s considered the father of existentialism, which stresses individual freedom, self-creation and personal responsibility. It is no surprise, then, that love is a central focus of his work. What he called “ethical” love expands freedom, while “aesthetic” love restricts it.

Aesthetic love

In 1843, a young Kierkegaard published “Either/Or,” his first book of philosophy – and one of his most important. The two volumes were published under the pseudonym “Victor Eremita,” one of many that Kierkegaard used throughout his life.

“Either/Or” makes a distinction between “aesthetic” and “ethical” ways of living. The aesthetic life is focused mainly on personal pleasure, while the ethical life expands to an awareness of how actions affect others.

Each way of life has its own form of love. Aesthetic love is one that you “fall” into. It comes over you. It is a powerful, seemingly irresistible force. The aesthetic lover “desires the individual absolutely,” Kierkegaard wrote.

Some lasting love begins that way, too. But aesthetic love lacks the trust and respect needed for stability. The yardstick of good and bad, right and wrong is centered on feelings and desires, not principles.

Feeling connected to and dependent on someone you don’t trust creates the tumult of addictive love. It can destroy the lover and the beloved, but often neither wants to give it up.

A counselee of mine fell instantly and madly in love. The passion was unlike anything he’d ever experienced. Though he doubted that the relationship could last, he told me he’d give up everything just to ride the wave for a year, or even six months. He was in the process of upending his life to be with her when the relationship failed a few months later. He went to a very dark place, doubting himself and the world.

This was a textbook example of Kierkegaard’s “aesthetic” love, which he talked about as an obsession or compulsion. In today’s terms, I’d consider it similar to addiction: a pattern that we feel compelled to continue, despite knowing how much it hurts us and others around us. Psychologists and philosophers debate how to define “addiction,” and whether love can become one, but research indicates there can be similarities in behavior and brain activity between the two.

Obsessive, compulsive love often uses the relationship to escape the lover’s own issues. He or she may seem besotted with their beloved. In reality, though, they see the beloved as an object that can fill their emptiness or resolve their angst, rather than an independent human being with his or her own needs and desires.

At its root, Kierkegaard writes, aesthetic love is “a kind of despair,” rooted in estrangement from oneself, a kind of self-rejection or self-deception.

Obsessing over someone can serve to distract us from our self-rejection and emptiness. Aesthetic love seeks freedom through the other person, rather than freely loving them.

Ethical love

For Kierkegaard, there is an alternative: ethical love, rooted in virtue, choice and a solid sense of self. Kierkegaard discusses this kind of love in the second volume of “Either/Or” and in “Works of Love,” a book he published in 1847 under his own name.

Kierkegaard maintains that ethical love lacks the obsession and compulsion of aesthetic love. It is rooted in self-awareness, conscious choices and freedom, not thoughtless desire.

Ethical love is, in short, an ongoing conscious commitment, independent of the ebb and flow of emotion. This holds for all love, romantic or otherwise. Love is “a matter of conscience,” not impulse or calculation, Kierkegaard wrote in “Works of Love.”

It should be based on respect: treating other people as ends in and of themselves, not means to our own ends. In addition, ethical love is anchored in trust. Without these foundations, only the illusion of intimacy is possible.

Love centered on principles, not feelings, may sound like duty. But for Kierkegaard, it was freeing. No one should accept mistreatment: “Duty alone makes for genuine freedom. Spontaneous love makes a man free and in the next moment dependent,” he wrote.

This paradoxical view results from his idea that we must use our freedom to become ourselves, a concept he develops in his philosophy of existentialism. He maintains that human beings need an anchor in something greater than ourselves to fully utilize our freedom. Ultimately, for Kierkegaard, this was a personal God, but his insights can be illuminating even without reference to God.

Kierkegaard stresses that ethical love liberates not only the lover but the beloved: “The highest that one human being can do for another is to make him free, to help him stand alone.” This kind of love isn’t the joining of two into one – that is the enmeshment of obsessive, compulsive, addictive love. Ethical love is between two individual human beings who have chosen to trust, respect, support and forgive one another.

The distinction between the illusion of love and real love has a long history. Kierkegaard provides insight into how to effectively tell the difference – and how the power of real love lies in mutual liberation.

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-20 13:44 UTC

item.title: El Niño created a skiers’ paradise in Chile – now it’s Sierra Nevada and Southern Rockies’ turn
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

El Niño has a reputation for being a skier’s dream, bringing lots of snow to California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season. But El Niño’s supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.

I’m an avid skier and snow scientist at Colorado State University. As the U.S. snow season begins amid what’s forecast to be one of the strongest El Niños on record, let’s take a look at what Chile’s very snowy winter might tell North America about what’s to come.

The pros and cons of all that precipitation

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon that raises global temperatures and shifts weather patterns around the world.

It is defined by rising surface temperatures in the east-central tropical Pacific Ocean. When temperatures there are at least 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 Fahrenheit) warmer than average for three months, the world is in El Niño. The August-October average was 2.5 C warmer (36.5 F, making this among the warmest periods on record going back to 1950.

In the U.S., the southern half of the country tends to be wetter than usual during strong El Niños. That happens because the Pacific jet stream shifts southward, steering storms with it. The northern tier of the U.S. tends to be drier and warmer than normal.

That pattern is almost exactly what’s being forecast for the U.S. winter of 2026-27. It’s also what the U.S. Southwest is already experiencing – to the extreme.

Powerful storms supercharged by El Niño in October and November caused widespread destructive flooding in the Four Corners region of New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and Utah. Fast-melting snow and days of heavy rain flooded the San Juan River and Rio Grande, damaging hundreds of homes.

Recovering from last year’s snow drought

Community water systems and farms across the West need that precipitation after last winter delivered one of the lowest snow years on record for almost the entire western United States.

Major reservoirs in the Colorado River basin dropped during the year to their lowest levels since they were first filled. The two biggest – Lake Powell and Lake Mead – together supply water for about 40 million people and hydropower for hundreds of thousands of people.

The very low snowfall, as well as unusually warm midwinter temperatures that drove sublimation – the evaporation of snow – reduced water stored in the mountains. And that was followed by record-high summer temperatures.

Fall 2026’s heavy rain and snow may help make up for last year and start to alleviate a long-running drought that has been causing water supply problems across the western U.S. for a quarter century.

In a positive sign, Lake Powell rose with the recent rains. Overall, the Super El Niño conditions being forecast for 2026-27 are expected to bring more than average rain and snow this winter across much of the southern and central United States, where it’s also likely to alleviate drought.

What happens in Chile …

Snow scientists like me keep an eye on the South American winter in El Niño years like this because it can give us a sense of what’s coming for North America.

Keep in mind that El Niño has been strengthening over the past few months – including through the South American winter that just ended.

South America saw a huge amount of snow, particularly in the central Chilean Andes. In some areas like Portillo, the snow accumulation was the deepest since the current drought began in 2010, and the deepest in the past 70 years north of Santiago at the top of the Limarí River.

The snow was a boon for Chile’s ski resorts. Valle Nevado got over 24 feet (7.3 meters) of snow and extended its ski season, originally scheduled to end in early October, into early December. Even the extremely dry Atacama Desert saw widespread snow followed by an explosion of spring flowers.

Historically, snowy winters in Chile have meant snowy winters for California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies, too. The warm El Niño ocean allows the atmosphere to pick up more moisture in this zone than usual, and this brings snowstorms to the U.S. Southwest.

If that pattern holds this winter, the southern and central parts of the West should see well-above-average snowpack and active ski seasons, and those dangerously depleted reservoirs will have a chance to at least partially refill.
